title: Can you solve these 13 case interview maths questions in your head?
description: Practice sums for case interviews: margins, percentages, growth and big numbers, with worked answers hidden until you are ready.
hook: Yes, if you know a dozen formulas and a few shortcuts: every question below can be done in your head in under a minute. Try each one out loud, as you would in an interview, then open the model answer to check both the number and the method.
body:
How to use this set

Treat each question as if an interviewer had just asked it. Say the formula first, then the arithmetic, then a one-line check, then what the number means. Time yourself: under 30 seconds is good for the simple ones, under 60 for the two-step ones. If you miss one, redo it the next day rather than rereading the answer.

A good spoken answer has four beats:

"Break-even is fixed costs over contribution per unit (formula). Contribution is $25 minus $10, so $15, and $3M over $15 is 200,000 units (arithmetic). Check: 200,000 times $15 is $3M (check). So they need to sell 200,000 units before the line makes money (so what)."

A weak answer gives only the middle beat, quietly, and leaves the interviewer to work out whether it is right. The formulas are all in the 20 formulas explained if you need a refresher.

Margins, break-even and payback

1. A product costs $40 and sells for $50. What is the margin? The markup?

Show the answer

Profit per unit is $50 − $40 = $10. Margin is profit over price: $10 ÷ $50 = 20%. Markup is profit over cost: $10 ÷ $40 = 25%. Markup is always the bigger number, because cost is smaller than price. If you ever get a markup below the margin, you have swapped the denominators.

2. Fixed costs are $3M, the price is $25 and the variable cost is $10. What is break-even volume?

Show the answer

Contribution per unit is $25 − $10 = $15. Break-even is $3M ÷ $15 = 200,000 units. Check: 200,000 × $15 = $3M. The natural next question is how long it takes to sell 200,000 units, which turns break-even into a payback period.

3. A machine costs $1.2M and saves $300k a year. What is the payback period?

Show the answer

Payback is investment over yearly saving: $1.2M ÷ $300k = 4 years. Cancel the zeros first: 1,200 ÷ 300 = 4. Then compare with the machine's useful life and the client's target. A four-year payback on a machine that lasts ten years is attractive; on one that lasts five, it is marginal.

4. A retailer marks its goods up by 50% on cost. What is its margin?

Show the answer

Pick a cost of $100. A 50% markup gives a price of $150 and a profit of $50. Margin is $50 ÷ $150 = 33.3%. The general rule: margin = markup ÷ (1 + markup), so 0.5 ÷ 1.5 = one third. Choosing a $100 cost makes any markup question easy.

Growth and value

5. Revenue grows from $50M to $80M over five years. Roughly what is the CAGR?

Show the answer

End ÷ start is 80 ÷ 50 = 1.6. Test 10%: 1.1⁵ = 1.61, which is almost exactly 1.6. So the CAGR is about 10% (9.9% precisely). The common mistake is 60% ÷ 5 = 12%, which ignores compounding and overstates the rate. See compound growth and CAGR for more.

6. A business generates $5M a year forever. At an 8% discount rate, what is it worth today?

Show the answer

Perpetuity value is cash flow ÷ discount rate: $5M ÷ 0.08 = $62.5M. To do it in your head, 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, then multiply by 100. Check: 8% of $62.5M is $5M a year, which is exactly the cash flow.

7. Price rises 10% and volume falls 5%. What happens to revenue?

Show the answer

Revenue is price × volume, so multiply the factors: 1.10 × 0.95 = 1.045. Revenue rises 4.5%. The shortcut 10% − 5% = 5% is close but slightly high, because it ignores the cross-term (10% × 5% = 0.5%). Then ask about profit: the lower volume also cuts variable costs, so profit rises by more than revenue does.

8. A launch has a 50% chance of making $10M, a 30% chance of $2M and a 20% chance of losing $5M. What is the expected value?

Show the answer

Multiply each outcome by its probability and add: 0.5 × $10M = $5M, 0.3 × $2M = $0.6M, 0.2 × −$5M = −$1M. Total $5M + $0.6M − $1M = $4.6M. Check the probabilities sum to 100% first (50 + 30 + 20 = 100). A positive expected value supports launching, but say whether the client can survive the 20% chance of a $5M loss.

Percentages and big numbers

9. What is 17% of 340?

Show the answer

10% is 34. 1% is 3.4, so 7% is 23.8. Total 34 + 23.8 = 57.8. To check the size, 17% is just over a sixth (16.7%), and 340 ÷ 6 is about 57. Percentages in your head covers this method.

10. What is 15% of 480?

Show the answer

10% is 48 and 5% is half of that, 24. Total 48 + 24 = 72. Ten plus five is the fastest route to any 15% and is the same method you use for a tip.

11. A market is worth $4.5B and has 1.5M customers. What is the spend per customer?

Show the answer

Cancel the zeros first. A billion is a thousand million, so $4.5B ÷ 1.5M = 4,500 ÷ 1.5 = $3,000 per customer. Check by multiplying back: 1.5M × $3,000 = $4.5B. Multiplying big numbers explains how to keep track of the zeros.

Customers and subscriptions

12. Monthly churn is 2%. What is the average customer lifetime?

Show the answer

Average lifetime is roughly 1 ÷ churn: 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 months, just over four years. Keep the units matched: monthly churn gives a lifetime in months. And 2% a month is not 24% a year: because churn compounds on a shrinking base, 0.98¹² = 0.785, so about 21.5% of a cohort leaves within a year.

13. A subscription business has 80,000 customers paying $15 a month. In one month it adds 5,000 customers and loses 4% of its opening customers. How many customers does it end with, and what is its monthly recurring revenue at the end of the month?

Show the answer

Churned customers: 4% of 80,000 = 3,200, calculated on the opening base. Closing customers: 80,000 + 5,000 − 3,200 = 81,800. Closing monthly recurring revenue: 81,800 × $15 = $1,227,000, about $1.23M. Two traps: applying churn to the closing base, and calling this figure "revenue earned this month". It is a snapshot at month end (a stock); the revenue actually earned during the month depends on when customers joined and left (a flow). Say which one you mean.

What your mistakes tell you

  • Wrong by a factor of 10 or 1,000 (questions 6, 11): write the zeros down separately and convert units before you divide.
  • Slightly too high on growth (questions 5, 7): you added percentages instead of multiplying factors.
  • Margin and markup swapped (questions 1, 4): say the denominator out loud every time.
  • Right number, slow: you are calculating from scratch things you should know by heart. Learn the fraction table on the case maths cheat sheet.

Where to practise next

For timed practice with fresh numbers every time, use the case maths drill. To practise the same skills inside a full case, with an exhibit and a recommendation at the end, pick a case from the casebook. And for the routine of staying calm while you calculate out loud, read how to do case maths without panicking.
